rules.summary: Borrow when a callee only needs temporary access; clone when the API genuinely needs an independent owned value
Accept borrowed views such as `&[T]`, `&str`, and `&Path` when the implementation only needs a view
Use `Cow<'a, B>` when an API can usually borrow data but sometimes needs an owned value
Use `Arc<T>` when multiple owners may cross thread boundaries; add synchronization only for mutation that actually requires it
Use `Rc<T>` for shared ownership that is confined to one thread
Use `RefCell<T>` when thread-local shared access genuinely needs runtime-checked interior mutability
Use the right `Mutex<T>` for the execution model: `std`/`parking_lot` for synchronous code, `tokio::sync::Mutex` for async code
Choose `RwLock<T>` when concurrent readers materially help the measured workload, not from a fixed read/write ratio
Implement `Copy` for small, simple types
Use `Clone` to make non-`Copy` duplication explicit, but do not infer a universal allocation or cost model from `.clone()`
Borrow large values when ownership transfer is unnecessary; use indirection when it solves a real layout, location, or ownership problem—not from a fixed byte threshold
Rely on ordinary lifetime elision where it applies; treat Edition-2024 RPIT capture as a separate rule
Use `Cell::update` (Rust 1.88+) for concise single-threaded read-transform-write updates on `Copy` values
Edition 2024 simplifies RPIT returns whose hidden type borrows; it does not change ordinary `Cow<'_, T>` return elision
Use `core::range::Range` (Rust 1.96+) when `Copy` range values are useful; keep `core::ops::Range` for legacy iterator and API interoperability
Use `LazyLock` for thread-safe lazy statics and `LazyCell` for local or thread-local lazy values; use `OnceLock`/`OnceCell` when initialization is imperative rather than tied to one initializer
Use `thiserror` to derive typed library errors when it removes boilerplate without hiding the API
Use `anyhow` at application boundaries when callers need context and reporting more than a stable typed error API
Use `Result<T, E>` for fallible operations; encode invariants explicitly and keep deliberate termination at the application boundary
Add context at abstraction boundaries so an error says what operation failed as well as why
Avoid `unwrap()` and `expect()`; preserve failures explicitly and encode invariants in types
Avoid `expect()` even for invariants; encode the invariant, propagate failure, or terminate deliberately at the process boundary
Use `?` when a fallible operation should short-circuit through the surrounding error context
Implement specific `From<SourceError>` conversions when the conversion is unconditional, unambiguous, and preserves the information callers need
Preserve underlying causes in the error source chain
Keep `Error` display messages concise, usually lowercase, and usually without trailing punctuation so they compose cleanly
Document meaningful `Err` conditions in a `# Errors` section
Define domain error types when callers benefit from knowing what failed
Do not use Clippy's `allow-unwrap-types` to punch type-wide holes in a strict no-unwrap/no-expect policy
Use `#[diagnostic::do_not_recommend]` on trait impls whose appearance in diagnostics would mislead users

Prefer narrow, reasoned `#[expect(...)]` when a suppressible lint reliably fires; use a narrow reasoned `#[allow(...)]` only when lint activation is configuration-dependent and fulfillment semantics cannot work
Use `core::error::Error` for genuine `no_std` error types; current `thiserror` supports this on Rust 1.81+
`try {}` blocks remain nightly-only; prefer stable `Result`/`Option` contexts unless the scoped expression is worth the nightly dependency
Pre-allocate when you have a useful size bound
Use `SmallVec` when collections are usually small but may grow
Use `ArrayVec<T, N>` when a hard capacity belongs in the type
Consider indirection when one enum variant makes every enum value much larger, but measure the workload before paying for a heap allocation
Use `Box<[T]>` when owned heap data has a fixed length and you do not need spare capacity or growth operations
Use `ThinVec<T>` when a pointer-sized collection handle is valuable
Use `Clone::clone_from` when repeatedly replacing an existing value and the concrete type can profitably reuse its resources
Reuse collection capacity across repeated temporary workloads when allocation behavior or profiling shows it is worthwhile
Avoid creating an intermediate `String` with `format!` when the caller can use a literal, formatting arguments, or an existing output buffer directly
Write formatting directly into the real destination when an intermediate owned `String` would only be copied elsewhere
Use bump arenas when many values share one lifetime and bulk deallocation is more useful than individual destruction
Use zero-copy patterns with slices and `Bytes`
Consider compact or clone-on-write string types when string representation is a measured memory or allocation bottleneck
Use appropriately-sized integers to reduce memory footprint
Assert type size when it is a real ABI, memory-budget, or measured performance constraint; prefer upper bounds when exact layout is not required
Use `mem::take` / `mem::replace` to move a value out of a `&mut` without cloning
Know Rust's deterministic destruction order, and make resource dependencies explicit when one value must outlive another
Prefer `Arc<str>` over `Arc<String>` for thread-shared immutable strings
Use `Box::new_uninit()` when you genuinely need deferred or in-place heap initialization; call `assume_init()` only after the allocation contains a valid `T`
Consider `EcoString` for clone-heavy immutable-or-COW strings
Profile memory before optimizing
Use `SlotMap` for generation-checked stable keys; use `DenseSlotMap` when densely stored values and fast iteration are important
Write a `// SAFETY:` comment above every `unsafe` block and a `# Safety` section in every `unsafe fn`.
Keep `unsafe` blocks as small as possible — mark only the operation that requires unsafety, not the surrounding safe code.
Run `cargo miri test` in CI for every crate that contains `unsafe` code.
Use `MaybeUninit<T>` for uninitialized memory; never use `mem::uninitialized()` or `mem::zeroed()` for types with validity invariants.
In Rust 2024, use `unsafe extern { }` blocks and mark an item `safe` only when every safe Rust caller can satisfy its contract.
Justify manual `Send`/`Sync` from invariants enforced by the type and its dependencies, not from hoped-for caller behavior
In Rust 2024, write `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`, `#[unsafe(export_name = "...")]`, and `#[unsafe(link_section = "...")]` — not the bare attribute forms.

Prefer strict provenance APIs (`ptr.addr()`, `ptr.map_addr()`, `ptr.with_addr()`) over integer-pointer round-tripping (`as usize` / `as *const T`); prefer raw borrow syntax (`&raw const x` / `&raw mut x`) over `addr_of!` / `addr_of_mut!`.
Use a builder when construction has several optional settings, validation, or staged configuration
Mark consuming builder methods or the builder type `#[must_use]` when ignoring the returned builder is likely a bug
Use newtypes when identical representation hides meaning the compiler should distinguish
Use typestate when compile-time state transitions materially simplify or strengthen an API
Seal a public trait when downstream crates should be able to use it but not implement it
Use a local extension trait when method-call syntax on an external type materially improves an API
Parse weakly typed input into invariant-bearing domain types at system boundaries instead of repeatedly validating primitives downstream
Accept `Into<T>` when the API intentionally takes ownership and useful caller types can convert into `T`
Use `AsRef<T>` for cheap generic borrowed views when accepting several source types is genuinely useful
Add `#[must_use]` when silently discarding a value is plausibly a bug; rely on the built-in `unused_must_use` semantics instead of treating every return value alike
Use `#[non_exhaustive]` when a public struct, enum, or enum variant is intentionally open to compatible growth
Implement `From<Source> for Destination` for clear infallible conversions you own; use `Into<Destination>` primarily as a caller-side bound
Implement `Default` only when the type has a sensible canonical default value
Implement standard traits when their semantics are useful and appropriate for the public type
Make serde optional in general-purpose libraries when serialization is not part of the core API
Implement `FromIterator` and `Extend` for collection types, and `IntoIterator` for all three reference forms
Overload operators only when the semantics are natural and unsurprising
Use `bon` when typestate builders for structs or functions improve the API; account for proc-macro and typestate compile cost
Use `#[diagnostic::do_not_recommend]` on legal trait impls whose appearance in diagnostics would usually mislead callers
Use `nutype` when generated sanitization, validation, and invariant-preserving trait impls materially simplify a public newtype API
Start with Tokio's default runtime configuration; choose runtime flavor and tuning from execution requirements and measurements
Keep blocking lock guards out of awaited sections; use an async mutex when exclusive access itself must span `.await`.
Use `spawn_blocking` for blocking synchronous work; bound CPU-heavy work or use a dedicated CPU pool such as Rayon
Use `tokio::fs` for ordinary filesystem operations from async code; use dedicated async types for pipes/devices and other special files
Use `CancellationToken` when tasks need explicit cooperative cancellation
Use `join!` / `try_join!` for a fixed set of independent futures; they run concurrently on one task, not in parallel by themselves
Use `try_join!` for a fixed set of fallible futures that should run concurrently and stop when one returns an error
Use `tokio::select!` to wait on several async events, while reasoning explicitly about cancellation of the losing futures
Prefer bounded channels when backlog growth must be constrained; use unbounded channels only when an external invariant bounds the backlog.
Use `tokio::sync::mpsc` when an async task needs a single-consumer message queue with Tokio-aware waiting or backpressure
Use `tokio::sync::broadcast` for bounded fan-out where every active subscriber should observe each retained event.
Use `watch` when receivers need the latest state, not a lossless history of every update
Use `tokio::sync::oneshot` when exactly one value should travel from one sender to one receiver, especially for actor-style request-response.
Use `JoinSet` to track a dynamic collection of Tokio tasks when completion order and lifecycle control matter
Do not clone merely because an `.await` exists; clone or move ownership when a task/lifetime boundary actually requires ownership.
Use native `async fn` in traits for static dispatch when its return-future bounds fit the API
Use `AsyncFn`/`AsyncFnMut`/`AsyncFnOnce` bounds instead of `F: Fn() -> Fut, Fut: Future`
Ensure futures used in `tokio::select!` branches are cancellation-safe
Detect async worker stalls with latency/console instrumentation; treat blocking-pool metrics as pool pressure, not proof that async workers are blocked
Use Tokio runtime metrics as scheduler telemetry, and distinguish stable metrics from `tokio_unstable` instrumentation
Combine `JoinSet` + `CancellationToken` + `select!` for structured async task management
Use rayon's `par_iter()` for CPU-bound data parallelism
Use `std::thread::scope` to borrow stack data across threads
Use the weakest correct memory `Ordering` for every atomic operation
Prefer `thread_local!` with `Cell`/`RefCell` over `static mut`
Use `#[inline]` selectively, especially when a small non-generic public function benefits from cross-crate inlining.
Treat `#[inline(always)]` as a strong optimization hint, not a command; use it only when measurement justifies it.
Use cold-path and inlining annotations as measured optimization hints, not source-level guarantees
Use `#[cold]` or `core::hint::cold_path()` only when an unlikely path is known or measured to matter.
Use `cold_path()` and `select_unpredictable` for branch hints on stable Rust
Enable LTO in release builds
Set `codegen-units = 1` for maximum optimization in release builds
Use Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO) for maximum performance
Tune `target-cpu` only for deployment CPUs you actually control, and use explicit runtime dispatch for portable binaries
Structure hot loops so bounds are easy to prove; verify optimized code before using unchecked indexing
Start with autovectorization; use stable SIMD crates or carefully dispatched `#[target_feature]` code when measurement justifies it.
Shape data around measured access patterns and working sets; do not assume one layout is universally cache-friendly
Use `core::hint::cold_path()` to mark unlikely inline paths (Rust 1.95+)
Use `core::hint::select_unpredictable()` for branchless conditional moves (Rust 1.88+)
Handle integer overflow explicitly: `checked_`/`saturating_`/`wrapping_`/`overflowing_`
Avoid `as` for narrowing casts; use `From` for widening and `TryFrom` for narrowing
Use approximate comparison when you mean numerical closeness; use exact equality for exact semantics and `total_cmp` for total ordering
Bound values with `clamp` and saturating arithmetic
Use `NonZero*` types to forbid zero and unlock the niche optimization
Wrap semantically distinct IDs in distinct types, and encode additional invariants such as non-zero values at construction
Put durable domain invariants behind checked constructors so downstream code can rely on the type instead of re-validating primitives
Use enums when a value is in exactly one of several mutually exclusive states
Use `Option<T>` when absence is an ordinary state; use `Result<T, E>` when callers need failure information
Use `Result<T, E>` when an operation can fail with useful error information
Use `PhantomData` for zero-cost type markers
Use `!` as the return type of functions that never return normally
Put each trait bound on the API surface that actually requires it
Replace durable stringly-typed states and identifiers with enums or domain types, while keeping text parsing at system boundaries
Use `#[repr(transparent)]` when a wrapper intentionally needs the wrapped field's layout and ABI
Implement `Deref`/`DerefMut` only for smart-pointer and transparent wrapper types
Use `Display` for user-facing output and `Debug` for diagnostics; never swap them
Implement `LowerHex`, `UpperHex`, `Octal`, and `Binary` for numeric newtypes
Use `derive_more` to remove mechanical trait boilerplate when the generated trait semantics are actually part of your API
Use `#[repr(transparent)]` only when a newtype intentionally promises the wrapped field's layout or ABI
Use `NonZero<T>` when zero is invalid, and use only operations whose result semantics preserve that invariant
Use validated newtypes to make invalid states unrepresentable; `nutype` is useful when generated constructors and invariant-preserving trait impls justify a proc macro
Use an associated type when each impl has exactly one output type; use a generic parameter when a type can implement the trait for many input types
Use a blanket impl `impl<T: Bound> Trait for T` to give behaviour to every type that satisfies a bound
Respect the orphan rule; wrap a foreign type in a newtype to implement a foreign trait on it
Define a trait in terms of a few required methods plus defaulted ones built on top of them
Choose static dispatch (generics / `impl Trait`) vs dynamic dispatch (`dyn Trait`) deliberately
Keep a trait dyn-compatible (object-safe) when you need `dyn Trait`
Use trait-object upcasting for dyn-compatible supertrait relationships (Rust 1.86+)
Implement `TryFrom` for fallible conversions instead of ad-hoc conversion functions
Implement `FromStr` to enable `str::parse` for string-to-type conversions
Accept `impl AsMut<T>` for flexible mutable borrowed inputs instead of concrete mutable references
Use inline `const { }` blocks for compile-time evaluation and assertions
Make functions `const fn` when they can run at compile time
Parameterize over values with const generics `<const N: usize>`
Use `const` for an inlined value and `static` for a single addressed instance
Match the external naming convention with `#[serde(rename_all = ...)]`
Use `#[serde(default)]` for optional and backward-compatible fields
Omit empty fields with `skip_serializing_if`
Inline nested structs or capture extra keys with `#[serde(flatten)]`
Choose enum tagging deliberately: externally, internally, adjacently tagged, or untagged
Reject unexpected keys with `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`
Customize a field's (de)serialization with `with` / `serialize_with` / `deserialize_with`
Validate while deserializing with `#[serde(try_from = "Raw")]`
Use `let ... else` for early-return pattern extraction
Use `matches!()` for boolean pattern tests
Use `if let` / `while let` chains to combine pattern bindings and conditions
Match owned enums exhaustively; avoid catch-all `_` that hides new variants
Use `@` bindings to capture a value while matching it against a pattern
Reach for a macro only when a function or generic cannot express it
Understand `macro_rules!` mixed-site hygiene and use `$crate` for defining-crate paths
Capture with precise fragment specifiers, not raw `:tt`, where you can
Use `#[macro_export]` when a `macro_rules!` macro is part of the public crate API
Route exported-macro support items through a clearly marked `#[doc(hidden)]` module when call-site visibility requires them to be public
Put procedural macros in a dedicated `proc-macro = true` crate and re-export them from the ordinary library facade
Put proc-macro parsing and generation in testable `syn`/`quote` helpers
Turn expected proc-macro input errors into spanned compile errors instead of panics
Require the least restrictive `Fn` trait a callback needs (`FnOnce` ⊇ `FnMut` ⊇ `Fn`)
Return closures as `impl Fn`/`FnMut`/`FnOnce`, not `Box<dyn Fn>`
Use `move` for closures that outlive the current scope; clone before `move` to keep the original
Accept `impl Fn` (generic) for hot callbacks; use `&dyn Fn`/`Box<dyn Fn>` to cut code size or to store them
Capture only what you use; lean on edition-2021 disjoint closure captures
Use async closures when a callback future needs to borrow from closure captures; use `AsyncFn*` bounds for higher-order async callbacks
Use `BinaryHeap` for a priority queue or repeated max-extraction
Pick the map by access pattern: `HashMap` (fast, unordered), `BTreeMap` (sorted / range queries), `IndexMap` (insertion order)
Default to `Vec`; use `VecDeque` for queue/deque behaviour; avoid `LinkedList`
Use `HashSet`/`BTreeSet` for membership tests and dedup, not linear `Vec::contains`
Use `UpperCamelCase` for structs, enums, traits, type aliases, and other type-level names
Use `UpperCamelCase` for enum variants
Use `snake_case` for functions, methods, variables, and modules
Use `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and statics
Keep lifetime parameter names short and lowercase; use `'a` by default and descriptive names such as `'src` when they add real meaning
Use concise `UpperCamelCase` type-parameter names—often `T`, `E`, `K`, `V`, but descriptive names are appropriate when they improve clarity
Use `as_` for free borrowed conversions
Use `to_` for ad-hoc conversions that do nontrivial work without consuming a non-Copy receiver
Use `into_` for ad-hoc conversions that consume an owned value and produce another owned representation
Omit `get_` for ordinary named getters; reserve `get` for APIs where “get the one obvious value” or validated/indexed access is the established operation
Name boolean methods as clear predicates; use `is_`, `has_`, `can_`, and similar prefixes when they match the question being answered
For collection-wide traversal, use the conventional `iter`, `iter_mut`, and `IntoIterator` ownership shapes
Implement `IntoIterator` delegation for `for` loop support
Name public iterator types after the methods or functions that produce them
In `UpperCamelCase`, treat acronyms as ordinary words: `HttpServer`, `Uuid`, `TcpStream`
Avoid `-rs`, `-rust`, `rust-`, and similar language-only affixes in crate/package names
Name Cargo features without placeholder words like `abc`, `use-abc`, or `with-abc`
Keep compound names in a consistent, idiomatic word order
Put unit tests in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { }` within each module
Use `use super::*;` in test modules to access parent module items
Put external-API integration tests in Cargo's `tests/` targets
Use descriptive test names that explain what is being tested
Structure tests with clear Arrange, Act, Assert sections
Use proptest for property-based testing
Use mockall for trait mocking
Put meaningful external dependencies behind replaceable boundaries when that improves testing
Use RAII for owned test resources; do not confuse cleanup with safe mutation of process-global state
Use `#[tokio::test]` for ordinary Tokio-driven async tests, and configure the runtime flavor only when the test needs it
Use `#[should_panic]` for tests whose success condition is a deliberate panic
Use `criterion` for benchmarking (or `divan` for simpler workflows)
Keep public documentation examples executable as doctests when practical
Use `loom` to exhaustively test lock-free and concurrent code
Use snapshot tests for complex output that humans should review as a whole
Use `assert_matches!` / `debug_assert_matches!` (Rust 1.96+) for pattern-based assertions
Use `cargo-llvm-cov` for LLVM-based code coverage
Use `cargo-fuzz` for fuzz testing critical functions
Use `insta` for snapshot/approval testing
Use `cargo-nextest` for faster execution and CI partitioning
Use `rstest` for parameterized tests, fixtures, and async test setup
Document the public API with rustdoc comments
Use inner doc comments (`//!`) to document a crate or module as a whole
Add focused `# Examples` sections when an example materially clarifies how to use the API
Document meaningful failure conditions in a `# Errors` section
Include `# Panics` section for functions that can panic
Document caller obligations with `# Safety`; justify local unsafe operations with `// SAFETY:` proofs
Give doctests a `Result`-returning context when demonstrating fallible operations; do not hide setup failure with unwrap/expect
Hide incidental doctest setup with `# ` while leaving the behavior users need to understand visible
Use intra-doc links for important relationships that rustdoc should resolve and validate
Cross-link related public types and operations when the links help readers navigate the API
Fill `Cargo.toml` metadata for published crates
Unify the README and crate root docs with `#![doc = include_str!("../README.md")]`

Use real `#[cfg(...)]` attributes for availability; when nightly rustdoc's `doc_cfg` is enabled, let `doc(auto_cfg)` surface those conditions and use `doc(cfg)` only when you need to override the displayed condition
Use `#[doc(hidden)]` only when a public item must remain callable but should be omitted from normal generated documentation
Use `#[doc = include_str!("...")]` when an external text file is intentionally part of an item's generated documentation
Account for Edition 2024 rustdoc doctest merging, `standalone_crate`, and source-relative nested includes
Use `tracing` for structured, span-aware diagnostics instead of `println!` or bare `log`
Reusable libraries should emit observability data without surprising callers by installing process-global logging or tracing state
Record structured key-value fields, not values interpolated into the message string
Use `#[tracing::instrument]` and spans to attach context to async tasks and requests
Use log levels meaningfully and filter with `EnvFilter` / `RUST_LOG`
Log errors with their full source chain, and log each error exactly once
Never log secrets or PII; redact or skip them
Prefer direct iteration when you are traversing values; use indexing when the index is part of the algorithm
Keep iterator pipelines lazy when streaming or short-circuiting is useful; collect only when ownership, reuse, sorting, indexing, or another concrete requirement needs a collection
Keep iterator pipelines lazy until you actually need an owned collection; materialize intermediate results when their semantics justify it
Use a map's entry API when one key lookup should decide both the occupied and vacant cases.
Use `drain` or `extract_if` when you need to remove owned elements while retaining the source collection's allocation; do not introduce an intermediate collection unless ownership requires one
Use `extend`, `extend_from_slice`, or `append` when adding a batch expresses the ownership you want; reserve explicitly when the final size is cheaply known
Use `Iterator::chain` when it expresses the traversal clearly; split or materialize only when measurement shows the chained iterator is a bottleneck
Reuse an existing destination with `clear()` + `extend()` on stable Rust; nightly `Iterator::collect_into` appends like `Extend::extend` and does not clear for you
Use `std::hint::black_box` in benchmarks when compile-time knowledge could make the measured work unrealistically disappear or specialize.
Optimize release profile settings
Measure representative workloads before choosing an optimization, then measure again after the change.
Use a faster hasher (`ahash` / `FxHashMap`) when DoS resistance is not needed
Wrap `Read`/`Write` in `BufReader`/`BufWriter` for many small operations
Use `<[T]>::array_windows` and `<[T]>::as_chunks` when a compile-time window or chunk size is useful
Use `Atomic*::update` and `try_update` for cleaner compare-and-update loops
Treat `Copy` ranges as an ownership and ergonomics choice, not an automatic performance optimization
Use `extract_if` when matching elements should be removed while their ownership is yielded to the caller.
Use compiler hint APIs only when their semantics match a measured hot path; they are advisory optimizations, not code-generation guarantees
Put reusable or directly importable application logic in a library target; keep binary entry points thin when that separation helps.
Prefer domain/feature-oriented modules when they keep code that changes together in one place
Keep small projects flat
Choose a consistent multi-file module layout; both `foo.rs` + `foo/` and `foo/mod.rs` are supported
Use the narrowest visibility that matches the intended module boundary; use `pub(crate)` for APIs shared across the crate but not exposed downstream
Use `pub(super)` when an item declared in a child module must be visible in its parent module scope
Use `pub use` to curate intentional public paths; do not expose internal module layout or dependency types accidentally.
Offer a small opt-in `prelude` only when callers repeatedly need the same coherent set of imports.
Use `src/bin/` for conventionally discovered additional binary targets
Use workspaces for large projects
Use workspace dependency inheritance for consistent versions across crates
Design Cargo features to be additive whenever feature unification can combine them
Declare `rust-version` (MSRV) in Cargo.toml and test it in CI
Keep `build.rs` deterministic, narrow its declared inputs, and write generated artifacts under `OUT_DIR`.
Use `[lints]` / `[workspace.lints]` for centralized lint configuration
Use `[workspace.package]` for shared metadata inheritance
Use `cargo publish --workspace` for native workspace publishing (Rust 1.90+)
Deny clippy::correctness and equivalent rustc lints
Enable clippy::suspicious for likely bugs
Enable `clippy::style` for established Rust idioms, while treating its suggestions as reviewable guidance rather than formatting law
Enable `clippy::complexity` to catch needlessly complicated expressions and operations
Enable `clippy::perf` for established performance anti-patterns; measure before adding optimizer hints
Enable clippy::pedantic selectively
Warn on missing documentation for public items
Document every unsafe operation with the invariant that makes it sound
Enable clippy::cargo for published crates
Run cargo fmt --check in CI
Configure lints at workspace level for consistent enforcement
Enable `unexpected_cfgs` and declare known cfgs to catch feature-gate typos
Enable `clippy::nursery` lints selectively and re-check group membership when the toolchain changes
Detect unused feature flags declared in Cargo.toml (`[lints.cargo]`, nightly-only)
Use Dylint for project-specific custom lints without forking clippy
Use the `rust_2024_compatibility` lint group and `cargo fix --edition` to audit edition-sensitive code before switching to Rust 2024
Use the `[lints]` table in `Cargo.toml` for canonical lint configuration (Rust 1.74+)
Track Clippy lints uplifted into rustc and adjacent compiler lint changes (Rust 1.86-1.99)
Avoid `unwrap()` and `expect()`; make failure handling or invariant representation explicit
Do not use `expect()` as a shortcut for either error handling or invariant enforcement
Do not clone merely to satisfy ownership when borrowing, moving, or deliberate sharing better matches the API
Do not hold blocking lock guards across `.await`; an async mutex may intentionally span `.await` when the protected resource must remain exclusively owned.
Prefer `&str` over `&String` when the API only needs string contents
Accept slices when an API only needs element access; accept `Vec` references when vector-specific capacity or length-changing operations are genuinely part of the contract
Don't use indexing when iterators work
Do not use panics as the API for expected runtime failures; keep deliberate termination and assertions explicit at their real boundary
Do not accidentally discard errors; make best-effort and discard semantics explicit
Introduce generics and traits when they express a stable semantic boundary; do not generalize code solely for hypothetical flexibility
Don't optimize before profiling
Prefer static polymorphism when one concrete type is sufficient; use `dyn Trait` deliberately when runtime type erasure and heterogeneous implementations are part of the design
Avoid unnecessary intermediate formatting allocations in measured hot paths; keep `format!` when a new owned `String` is the actual result you need
Keep iterator pipelines lazy when materialization adds no semantic value; collect only when you need owned storage, reordering, repeated access, or another collection operation
Don't use strings where enums or newtypes provide a meaningful domain type
Do not default to `Arc<Mutex<T>>` when ownership, channels, atomics, or another synchronization primitive better matches the state
Don't block or depend on asynchronous work completing from `Drop` of async types
Don't call `block_on` from code that is already running asynchronously
Implement `Deref` only when transparent target-like behavior is part of the type's intended API
Never use `unsafe impl Send` or `unsafe impl Sync` merely to silence auto-trait errors; each impl is a safety contract that other unsafe code may rely on
Rotate session IDs when authentication or privilege changes so a pre-authentication identifier cannot inherit elevated state.
